key_points.text: Compression makes files smaller, so they use less storage and transfer faster over the Internet (less bandwidth, quicker downloads).

Lossy compression removes data permanently, giving much smaller files; suits images, audio and video where some loss isn't noticed. Lossless compression keeps all the data; essential for text, program code and anything that must be restored exactly. Recommend one by asking whether exact data matters.
Run length encoding stores a run of repeated values as the value and a count (AAAAABB → 5A2B). It works well on data with long runs, such as simple images, but can make data with few repeats bigger.
Dictionary coding replaces repeated entries with short codes and stores a dictionary to translate them back. The dictionary is stored with the file, so it only saves space when entries repeat enough.
Encryption keeps data confidential when stored or sent: intercepted ciphertext is useless without the key.

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key: fast, but the key has to be exchanged securely, and anyone who intercepts it can decrypt everything. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a matching private key to decrypt, so no secret key ever needs sending, but it is slower.

Hashing is one-way. Passwords are stored as hashes: when a user logs in, their entry is hashed and compared with the stored hash, so the real password is never stored. Other uses: checking that data hasn't been changed, and finding data quickly in a hash table.

dont_confuse.text: Encryption vs hashing: encryption is two-way (decrypt with the key); hashing is one-way.
Compression vs encryption: compression makes data smaller; encryption makes it unreadable. Neither does the other's job.
Public vs private key: data is encrypted with the receiver's public key and decrypted with the receiver's private key.
